segments.narration: A field of giant stone jars nobody could safely excavate. More than two thousand of them, across the Xiangkhoang Plateau in Laos.
Up to three metres tall, six tonnes each, carved from solid rock. Nobody living remembers putting them there.
And archaeologists mostly couldn't get near them. Around two hundred and seventy million cluster bombs were dropped on this plateau. Roughly eighty million never went off.
Clearance work from two thousand four opened the sites. Optical dating put the jars in place as early as around twelve forty BC.
Inside and around them: human bone, beads, iron tools. They are funerary vessels, a plateau-sized graveyard, and what kept it a mystery was a war three thousand years too late.

verdicts.claim: The jars range from about 1 to 3 metres in height and weigh up to about six tonnes, carved from stone.
verdicts.note: 70% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article, including 2 number(s)

verdicts.claim: An estimated 270 million cluster bombs were dropped or dumped on the Plain of Jars and about 80 million failed to detonate, restricting archaeological access.
verdicts.note: Wikipedia: 'An estimated 270 million cluster bombs were dropped or dumped on the Plain of Jars, around 80 million of which failed to detonate', which restricted access until clearance from 2004.

verdicts.claim: Clearance operations from 2004 opened sites for study, and optically stimulated luminescence dating placed jars in position as early as about 1240 BC.
verdicts.note: 71% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article, including 2 number(s)

verdicts.claim: Excavations found human remains, beads and iron tools with the jars, and UNESCO inscribed them in 2019 as Iron Age funerary vessels.
verdicts.note: Colani's excavations recovered glass beads, spindle whorls and bronze and iron tools; UNESCO's 2019 inscription describes secondary funerary practice evidenced by associated human remains and burial goods.
